scope: Ranks 251–1500, resolved current similar-word teaching and typed recall. Includes retained baseline cards; do not infer no synonyms from unchanged status.
grading: Only exact headword/explicit alternatives pass after case/edge-punctuation normalization. Accent/spelling slips and recognized inflections get score-free correction opportunities, not immediate rejection. Dictionary-form recall is explicit. Cloze and recognition acceptance are separate. Broad main teaching examples may show a different legitimate sense from selected typed cue; classify teaching alignment separately from false facts.

sections.title: To send
sections.text: Enviar and mandar overlap for sending a letter. Mandar also means command; enviar does not carry that sense.

sections.title: To place
sections.text: Colocar, poner, situar and ubicar overlap for placing something. Their broader uses differ: poner has many change-of-state constructions, and situar/ubicar emphasize location.
examples: Coloca la mesa junto a la ventana.
Place the table next to the window.

sections.title: To remove
sections.text: Quitar and retirar overlap for removing something. Sacar specifically suggests taking it out of somewhere; not every removal has that direction.
examples: Retira el vaso de la mesa.
Remove the glass from the table.

sections.title: To show
sections.text: Mostrar and enseñar overlap when letting someone see something. Enseñar also means teach, which is a different use.

sections.title: To care for
sections.text: Cuidar and atender overlap in looking after someone. Atender can also mean attend to a request; asistir a means attend an event.

sections.title: To attend
sections.text: Asistir a and acudir a overlap for attendance. Atender usually means pay attention to or look after, rather than simply be present at an event.

sections.title: To contribute
sections.text: Aportar commonly takes the contribution as its object. Contribuir commonly uses a for the goal and con for what is contributed; the verbs are not mechanically interchangeable in a fixed sentence.

sections.title: To possess
sections.text: Poseer and tener overlap for possession. Tener is also used for age, sensations and obligations; those constructions do not all transfer to poseer.

sections.title: To transform
sections.text: Transformar expresses a change of form or nature. Cambiar is broader: a change need not amount to a transformation.
examples: Transforma el edificio en un museo.
She transforms the building into a museum.

sections.title: To change
sections.text: Cambiar, alterar and modificar overlap in changing an arrangement. Transformar implies a change in form or nature, which may be more substantial.

sections.title: To separate
sections.text: Separar and apartar overlap for moving things apart. Separar also divides a whole into parts; apartar emphasizes setting something aside.

sections.title: To drive
sections.text: Conducir and manejar overlap for driving a car; manejar is common for this use in much of the Americas. Manejar also means handle or manage.

sections.title: To reveal
sections.text: Revelar means make hidden information known. Descubrir can mean uncover it or discover it for oneself; learning a fact and announcing it are different events.

sections.title: To try
sections.text: Intentar takes an infinitive directly. Tratar de + infinitive also means try to; probar can mean test, taste or try something out.
examples: She tries to open the door.

sections.title: Goal
sections.text: Objetivo and meta overlap for an aim. Propósito also names an intention; the intended purpose and a measurable target need not be identical.

sections.title: Method
sections.text: Método and procedimiento overlap for a way of carrying out a task. Procedimiento often highlights the steps; método can describe the overall approach.

sections.title: Price
sections.text: Precio is the selling price. Costo/coste is a cost, and valor is value or worth; these amounts can differ.

sections.title: Cost
sections.text: Costo and coste both mean cost, with regional preferences. Gasto is expenditure: money actually spent or an expense.

sections.title: Task
sections.text: Tarea names a task; labor and trabajo can describe the work involved. Trabajo also names employment, while una tarea can be unpaid or schoolwork.

sections.title: Photograph
sections.text: Foto is a shortened form of fotografía and remains feminine: una foto. Fotografía also names photography as an activity or art.

sections.title: Ground
sections.text: Suelo, tierra and terreno overlap in ground-related senses. Tierra can mean soil or land; terreno emphasizes a tract or type of land, and suelo also means a floor. Both tierra and suelo fit the selected soil cue: earth that supports plant growth.

sections.title: Home
sections.text: Casa and hogar overlap for home. Vivienda emphasizes a dwelling or housing; hogar also evokes home life and can mean hearth.

sections.title: Car
sections.text: Coche, automóvil and carro can name a car, with regional preferences. Carro can also be a cart, so its meaning depends on place and context.

sections.title: Husband
sections.text: Marido and esposo both mean husband. Novio means boyfriend or groom and does not by itself mean husband.

sections.title: Dad
sections.text: Papá is a familiar form of padre. Papá has final stress; papa without the accent can mean potato or pope.

sections.title: Danger
sections.text: Peligro emphasizes danger; riesgo often emphasizes the possibility or exposure to harm. They overlap in ordinary speech but are distinguished in technical contexts. Both are accepted for these ordinary-language cues; no technical distinction is specified.
examples: There is a danger of fire.

sections.title: Memory
sections.text: Recuerdo is a specific memory. Memoria also names the faculty of remembering or stored information; those broader meanings do not all take recuerdo.
examples: Es un recuerdo de mi infancia.
It is a memory from my childhood.

sections.title: Victory
sections.text: Victoria and triunfo overlap for victory. Triunfo can also describe success more generally, without a specific opponent.

sections.title: Stage
sections.text: Etapa and fase overlap for stages of a process. Etapa also names a leg of a journey or race.

sections.title: Moment
sections.text: Instante and momento overlap for a short moment. Momento also means a particular time or occasion and need not imply an instant.

sections.title: Sound
sections.text: Sonido is sound in general. Ruido often means noise, especially unwanted or irregular sound; not every sound is ruido.
examples: Oigo un ruido en la calle.
I hear a noise in the street.

sections.title: Feeling
sections.text: Sentimiento and emoción overlap for emotional experience. Sensación often describes a bodily sensation or impression; those are not automatically emotions.

sections.title: Soul
sections.text: Alma and espíritu overlap in spiritual senses. Espíritu also names attitude or disposition; alma takes el in the singular but is feminine.
examples: She talks about the human soul.

sections.title: Spirit; soul
sections.text: Espíritu and alma overlap for soul or spirit. Espíritu also refers to attitude, disposition or a ghost; those senses need separate context.

sections.title: Soul
sections.text: Alma is feminine despite el alma in the singular. Espíritu overlaps in the spiritual-being sense but has other meanings.

sections.title: Rule
sections.text: Regla and norma overlap for a rule governing behavior. Regla also means ruler, and norma can be a customary norm rather than an explicit instruction.

sections.title: Language
sections.text: Lengua and idioma overlap for a named language. Lenguaje can describe the human faculty, a system of expression or a style of language; it need not identify a national language.

sections.title: Exhibition
sections.text: Exposición and muestra overlap for an exhibition. Muestra also means a sample, while exposición has senses of explanation and exposure.

sections.title: Environment
sections.text: Ambiente and entorno overlap for surroundings. Ambiente also names an atmosphere or mood; entorno emphasizes what surrounds a person or thing.

sections.title: Desire
sections.text: Deseo names a desire. Ganas is common in tener ganas de, meaning feel like doing something; voluntad also means will or willingness.

sections.title: Previous
sections.text: Anterior and previo overlap for something earlier. Anterior also describes a position at the front in anatomical or spatial uses.

sections.title: Simple
sections.text: Simple and sencillo overlap for uncomplicated. Sencillo also suggests plain or unpretentious; simple has other senses, including mere.

sections.title: Strange
sections.text: Extraño and raro overlap for strange. Raro also means rare; extraño can mean foreign or unfamiliar.

sections.title: Specific
sections.text: Específico, concreto, particular and determinado overlap in identifying something specific. Particular and determinado also have other meanings; concreto can mean concrete rather than abstract.

sections.title: Usual
sections.text: Habitual, normal and común overlap for what is usual. Normal can refer to a standard, and común can mean shared; neither always means frequent.

sections.title: Global
sections.text: Mundial and global overlap for worldwide scope. Global can also mean overall, considering something as a whole rather than worldwide.

sections.title: Serious
sections.text: Grave and serio overlap for a serious problem. Serio can also describe a person's sober manner, while grave can describe a low-pitched sound.

sections.title: Full
sections.text: Lleno describes something filled. Completo means complete, with nothing missing; pleno can mean full or complete in particular combinations, but does not replace lleno for every container.

sections.title: Happy
sections.text: Feliz and contento overlap for feeling happy or pleased. Feliz also describes a happy life or fortunate event, beyond a momentary feeling.

sections.title: Short
sections.text: Bajo describes low height, including a short person. Corto describes short length or duration; pequeño describes small size more generally.

sections.title: Legal
sections.text: Jurídico concerns law. Legal can mean relating to law or permitted by law; judicial specifically concerns judges and courts.

sections.title: Expert
sections.text: Experto is an expert. Especialista specializes in a field, and profesional practices an occupation; the labels overlap but do not guarantee the same expertise.

sections.title: Never
sections.text: Jamás and nunca overlap for never. Negative words following a verb usually combine with no: no viene nunca.

sections.title: Perhaps
sections.text: Quizá and quizás are spelling variants with the same meaning. Acaso can also mean perhaps but has distinct uses in questions and por si acaso.

sections.title: Currently
sections.text: Actualmente and ahora overlap for present time. Ahora can mean right now, while actualmente often covers the current period; actualmente does not mean actually.

sections.title: Really
sections.text: Realmente and verdaderamente overlap for really or genuinely. Actualmente means currently, so it does not substitute for actually in this sense.

sections.title: Also
sections.text: Asimismo and también overlap for also. Asimismo often links statements in formal writing; así mismo can mean in that same way, and a sí mismo means to oneself.

sections.title: Above
sections.text: Arriba describes an upper place or direction. Encima commonly uses de for above or on top of a named thing; sobre takes its complement directly.
examples: El libro está encima de la mesa.
The book is on top of the table.

sections.title: Even
sections.text: Incluso, adverbial hasta and aun can mean even. Hasta also means until or as far as; aún with an accent means still or yet.

sections.title: To request
sections.text: Solicitar and pedir request something. Preguntar asks a question; preguntar información does not substitute for pedir información.

sections.title: To laugh
sections.text: Reír means laugh; sonreír means smile. A smile does not necessarily involve laughter.

sections.title: To smile
sections.text: Sonreír means smile, while reír means laugh. They describe related but distinct actions.

sections.title: To notice
sections.text: Notar, advertir and percibir overlap for noticing a change. Advertir also means warn; perceiving something is not necessarily warning someone.

sections.title: To prevent
sections.text: Impedir and evitar overlap for preventing an event. Evitar also means avoid something without preventing it from existing.

sections.title: To avoid
sections.text: Evitar and esquivar overlap in avoiding an obstacle. Impedir means prevent or obstruct; it does not mean going around an obstacle oneself.

sections.title: To exhibit
sections.text: Exponer and mostrar overlap for displaying works. Exponer also means explain or expose to a risk; those uses require context.

sections.title: To recommend
sections.text: Recomendar and aconsejar overlap for recommending something. Aconsejar also concerns advice about actions.

sections.title: Police officer
sections.text: Policía names the police or an officer. Agente can also mean an officer when the context is police, but has broader meanings.

sections.title: Agent
sections.text: Agente can be a representative or a police officer. Policía fits the officer sense, not every kind of agent.

sections.title: Tomorrow
sections.text: Adverbial mañana means tomorrow, while ayer means yesterday. The noun mañana means morning.

sections.title: Instrument; tool
sections.text: Instrumento and herramienta overlap for a tool or implement. Instrumento also names a musical instrument or a formal document.

sections.title: Tool
sections.text: Herramienta and instrumento overlap for tools. Not every musical instrumento is called a herramienta in ordinary usage.

sections.title: To split
sections.text: Partir can mean split or depart. Salir overlaps with departure, not dividing an object.

sections.title: To take
sections.text: Coger commonly means take in Spain but has a vulgar sexual meaning in many American regions. Tomar is a widely usable alternative for taking.

sections.title: To arrange
sections.text: Ordenar can arrange things or give an order. Mandar overlaps with commanding, not simply arranging objects.

sections.title: Awareness
sections.text: Conciencia can be awareness or conscience. Conocimiento overlaps with knowing or awareness, not moral conscience.

sections.title: Knowledge
sections.text: Conocimiento is knowledge. Conciencia can express awareness or conscience, not all accumulated knowledge.

sections.title: Tax
sections.text: Impuesto is a tax. Tasa can be a rate or a particular fee; the legal categories vary and are not automatically interchangeable.

sections.title: Rate
sections.text: Tasa can mean a rate or fee. Impuesto is a tax, not a numerical rate itself.

sections.title: How
sections.text: Qué can intensify an exclamation before an adjective or adverb: qué bien. Cómo has different exclamatory constructions and is not a mechanical replacement.
